summary:
Abandoned but not Forgotten is an interactive web platform designed to preserve the legacy of inactive missions on the Moon and Mars. It integrates four connected experiences: a free-flight space simulator where users pilot a spacecraft, land directly on Mars and navigate around the Moon and Earth; 3D orbital visualization toward each spacecraft's real location; Postcards from Silence, a minigame where you control a drone to recover lost telemetry before signal loss; and an interactive archive featuring planetary maps and technical data sheets backed by NASA's NSSDCA archive.

It addresses the challenge by transforming dense technical records into an educational, immersive, and gamified experience. It is important because it redefines the value of decommissioned rovers, landers, and probes: they are not forgotten space junk, but scientific monuments whose impact deserves to be explored and preserved to inspire future generations.
details:
Abandoned but not Forgotten is an interactive web platform designed as a space-tracking console and educational simulator to preserve the legacy of inactive missions on the Moon and Mars. Organized into six connected sections, the platform guides users through an end-to-end exploration experience:

  • Signal Detection & Surface Expedition: Allow users to perform 3D exterior reconnaissance of six cataloged historic spacecraft: Surveyor 3, Apollo 11 EASEP, and Apollo 15 ALSEP on the Moon, alongside Opportunity (MER-B), InSight, and Ingenuity on Mars.
  • Field Simulator: Integrates two playable simulations: Flight to Mars & Descent, a two-stage 3D mission where users pilot a spacecraft from Earth past the Moon to reach Mars and execute a powered landing under real Martian gravity (3.72 m/s²) while managing fuel; and Postcards from Silence, a minigame where players pilot a reconnaissance drone within a critical 30-second uplink window to recover lost telemetry packets before signal loss.
  • Mission Context, Surface Archive & Sources & Credits: Provide a guided visual sequence, an interactive dashboard with filters, a planetary surface atlas, a timeline, and commemorative technical plaques verified against NASA's NSSDCA archive.

The creativity of our project lies in transforming dense technical records and historical data—which often go unnoticed by the general public—into a living telemetry station that blends storytelling, real physics, and gameplay rather than functioning as a static encyclopedia. This approach delivers clear benefits and measurable impact:

  • Broad accessibility: Compiled as a lightweight static web build, the platform runs smoothly in any standard browser without requiring heavy software installations or specialized hardware.
  • Reframing space heritage: It aims to shift public perception by showing that decommissioned rovers, landers, and surface stations are not space junk, but scientific monuments that paved the way for modern planetary science.
  • STEM inspiration and outreach: It sparks scientific curiosity among students and serves as an interactive educational resource for classrooms, planetariums, and science centers.

We developed the platform using a modern stack of web frameworks, 3D rendering engines, and game-packaging tools while prioritizing technical and scientific rigor:

  • Tools and languages: Astro 7, TypeScript, HTML5, CSS, and Tailwind CSS 4 for the static web architecture; Three.js and .glb 3D assets for orbital reconnaissance and the flight simulator; TurboWarp and the TurboWarp Packager to build and compile Postcards from Silence into standalone HTML5; along with Fontsource (Hanken Grotesk, Instrument Serif, JetBrains Mono), Node.js, Git, and GitHub.
  • Scientific accuracy and traceability: Every spacecraft record cites official NSSDCA IDs, real operational timelines, and verified physical parameters such as Martian surface gravity.
  • Scalability and license compliance: We built a modular architecture ready to expand with additional missions across the solar system, releasing our source code under the Apache License 2.0 while honoring NASA data guidelines and crediting all CC BY 4.0 3D models.
